strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem: combining inexpensive adaptation with quantized inference. Quantizing the merged base and LoRA weights removes the separate adapter inference path without QA-LoRA’s structural restrictions.

The evaluation covers six model configurations from 3B to 33B parameters, seven commonsense tasks, and zero-/five-shot MMLU at 3 and 4 bits. Several reported gains are substantial: on 3-bit LLaMA-2 7B, commonsense accuracy reaches 61.3%, versus 57.6% for QLoRA* and 56.3% for QA-LoRA.
The reported memory savings over conventional QAT are practically meaningful. For 7B models, L4Q uses 25.4 GB versus 79.5 GB for QAT and 41.9 GB for QAT-LoRA, approaching ordinary LoRA’s 25.1 GB.

The manuscript provides an algorithm, initialization/warm-up/rank ablations, training hyperparameters, and inference throughput by batch size. These details help assess the proposed accuracy–resource tradeoff.
weaknesses: The custom-backpropagation equations require correction or clarification. Equations (11) and (26)–(27) place an elementwise weight-clipping condition outside matrix products with different dimensions. With G = dL/dWq and M the weight-space clipping mask, the gradients should be alpha B^T(G ⊙ M) and alpha(G ⊙ M)A^T. This may be a notation error, but correctness of the central custom backward implementation needs verification.

Training comparisons contain consequential protocol ambiguities. Appendix E uses sequence length 128 specifically for L4Q’s 33B model, versus 2048 otherwise, confounding the largest-model memory and runtime comparisons. Figure 3 describes 100 training steps, whereas Appendix B describes 12,800 iterations with batch size 128; microsteps, optimizer updates, and gradient accumulation are not distinguished. These details are necessary for reproducibility.

Baseline evidence does not fully establish the broad superiority claims. Uniform QLoRA* and LoftQ* are reasonable hardware-controlled comparisons, but do not establish superiority over their original configurations. LoftQ* approaches chance-level MMLU at 3 bits, yet its training settings are missing from Table 8 and this collapse is not investigated. A fine-tune–merge–PTQ baseline would also directly test the claimed advantage over sequential adaptation and quantization.

Numerical reporting and uncertainty need attention. In Table 6, the rank-8 task scores average approximately 63.3%, rather than 62.7%, and rank-64 scores average 63.7%, rather than 63.2%. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals accompany often small accuracy differences. Superiority is also not universal: Table 3 reports 50.0% five-shot MMLU for L4Q on LLaMA-2 13B, below QLoRA*’s 50.6%.

The mechanistic explanation overstates the distinction from QAT-LoRA, which already jointly optimizes adapter and quantization parameters through a shared loss. Separate branches do not imply independent optimization. Controls sharing initialization and comparable backward-memory handling would better isolate the benefits of merging before quantization. Together with the gradient and protocol ambiguities, these unresolved evidentiary concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation despite the promising core contribution.
